 Minor child's income: When is it clubbed with parents' income and when is it taxed separately?
 SECTIONS Minor child's income: When is it clubbed with parents' income and when is it taxed separately? By Riju Mehta , ET Bureau Last Updated: Nov 16, 2026, 12:56:00 PM IST Rate Story Follow us Share Font Size Abc Small Abc Medium Abc Large Save Print Comment Synopsis Tax liability will depend on whether the child has earned it using his own skills, or the income is unearned. A minor can file an independent tax return through a parent or legal guardian acting as a ‘representative assessee’. The income clubbed with a parent’s income is generally disclosed in the parent’s return.

 ET Bureau Is your child skilled enough to start earning at a young age through sports competitions, YouTube, or perhaps an app that (s)he has developed? Even as you take pride in their accomplishments, make sure you understand the tax implications so that their income doesn’t become a liability for you or them. While many people don’t realise their kids’ income could be subject to taxation, others presume they don’t need to file any tax return for them.
 “Any income earned by a minor is subject to income tax in India, just like income earned by any other individual. However, the manner of taxation depends on the nature and source of such income,” says Kuldip Kumar, Partner, Mainstay Tax Advisors.
The income of a minor child can be broadly categorised into two types: income earned through their own efforts, skills, talent or specialised knowledge, and unearned income that is received as gifts, or in the form of returns from investments made by parents in the child’s name. “This is the distinction that decides whose tax it becomes. The income a minor earns through personal effort, an internship or part-time job, social media or YouTube, acting, modelling or freelancing is taxed in the minor’s hands at normal slab rates,” says Chandni Anandan, tax expert at ClearTax. 
In other cases, the minor’s income is generally clubbed with the income of the parent who earns more. “Where the parents’ marriage does not subsist, the minor’s income is clubbed with the income of the parent who maintains the child during the relevant tax year,” says Kumar. Parents can, however, avail of an exemption of up to Rs 1,500 per child for eligible clubbed income under the old tax regime. In case the minor child suffers from a disability specified in Section 99(1)(c)(iii), read with Section 154 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, their income is not clubbed with the income of either parent and is taxable in the hands of the minor.
 Provisions for taxation of minors

 All the Sections mentioned below are available in the old tax regime. 
 Exempt income
Gifts received from specified relatives are exempt from tax, irrespective of their value. So, a minor child is eligible for exemption for gifts received from specified relatives such as a brother or sister, brother or sister of parents, any lineal ascendant (maternal and paternal) or descendant, among others. However, gifts from friends or non-relatives may be taxable. If the aggregate amount of gift during a financial year exceeds Rs 50,000, the entire amount is taxable, not just the amount exceeding Rs 50,000,” says Kumar. Similar provisions apply to gifts of specified movable and immovable properties, subject to the prescribed valuation rules and thresholds.
 It is also important to distinguish between the gift and the income generated from the gifted amount. “Any interest or investment returns generated from such gifts are generally clubbed with the parent’s income,” says Sudhir Kaushik, Founder & CEO, Taxspanner, A Zaggle Company.
“Scholarships granted to meet educational expenses are also exempt without any monetary ceiling under Section 11, read with Schedule II (Serial no. 9),” says Kaushik. Similarly, payments received in cash or kind as awards or rewards are exempt under Section 11 read with Schedule II (Serial no. 10), provided the award is instituted in public interest by cen tral or state government, or by another body with the approval of the central government.
 Special tax
Under Section 194, the winnings from online games, cryptocurrency, virtual digital assets (VDAs), lotteries, crossword puzzles, races, card games, gambling or betting are subject to tax at a special rate of 30%. “These are taxed under a special, strict regime, regardless of the person’s age,” says Anandan.
This special rate comes with no basic exemption limit and deductions, and tax is usually deducted at source before the money reaches the winner. “So even a child with no other income cannot shelter these winnings under basic exemption,” says Anandan.

“In computing the income from VDAs, no deduction is permitted in respect of any expenditure or allowance, other than the cost of acquisition, if any. Further, losses arising from the transfer of VDAs cannot be set off against any other income or carried forward to subsequent tax years,” says Kumar. However, where cryptocurrency or any other VDA is received as a gift from a specified relative, it is exempt from tax, irrespective of its value.
The tax liability for some of the winnings depends on whether the income is skill-based or chance-based. Where the winning flows from the minor’s skill, such as competitive e-sports, it can fall within the skill-and-talent exception and be taxed in the minor’s hands. If it is chance-based, such as a lottery, it is clubbed with the parent’s income.
 Investments & savings
Under Section 99, interest, dividends and capital gains from investments in a minor’s name are ordinarily clubbed with the relevant parent’s income. “Simply investing in the child’s name does not shift the tax liability to the child,” says Kaushik. However, under Section 153, eligible taxpayers under the old tax regime may claim a deduction of up to Rs 10,000 for savings account interest. This deduction does not apply to ordinary fixed deposit or recurring deposit interest, says Kaushik.
“Parents may consider investing in the growth option of mutual funds rather than the dividend option, as this may defer the incidence of tax until redemption. However, the capital gains on redemption would be subject to the clubbing pro visions if redeemed by the minor before attaining majority,” says Kumar.
 Inheritance
Inheritance is not taxable as income in the hands of the recipient under the head ‘Income from Other Sources’, as Section 92 specifically excludes property received as inheritance. This exemption applies to minors as well. “However, when a minor earns income from inherited assets, it is subject to clubbing provisions under Section 99,” says Kumar. This is generally clubbed with the income of the parent whose total income is higher.
 Filing tax returns
A minor can file an independent tax return through a parent or legal guardian acting as a ‘representative assessee’. “This may be required where the minor earns taxable income through personal skills, exceeds the basic exemption limit, and statutory filing conditions apply. The income clubbed with a parent’s income is generally disclosed in the parent’s return,” says Kaushik. Even when a minor’s independent income falls below the basic exemption limit, filing a return may be desired to claim a refund of tax deducted at source.

 Failure to report income
When a minor’s income is clubbed with a parent’s income, the latter is legally responsible for reporting it in their own return. “Failure to disclose or misreport taxable income can result in additional tax, interest and penalties. Under Section 439, under-reporting may attract a penalty of 50% of the tax on under-reported income, while specified misreporting may attract 200%,” says Kaushik. “It can also result in reopening of past tax filings /assessments, subject to time limits, or scrutiny of investments into the source of funds and investments held in the minor’s name,” says Kumar.
